title: Bullish Posts $576 Million Q3 Profit, but Adjusted Earnings Were Just $18.7 Million
description:
Bullish reported $576.3 million in third-quarter net income, including a $598.4 million gain from revaluing its digital assets. However, nearly all of the result came from balance-sheet accounting rather than core exchange growth. 
The cryptocurrency exchange and information services group reported net income of $18.5 million a year earlier. For the latest quarter, diluted earnings per share reached $3.57, compared with $0.12 on an adjusted basis.
 Adjusted net income was $18.7 million, while trading volumes and both major revenue streams declined from the previous quarter. Despite the quarterly profit, Bullish recorded a net loss of $308.6 million for the first nine months of 2026. 
Trading and Non-Trading Revenue Decline
Bullish's trading volume and both major revenue streams declined from the second quarter, while lower operating expenses helped lift adjusted EBITDA. 
Subscriptions, services and other revenue remained roughly twice adjusted transaction revenue, continuing the pattern Finance Magnates reported after Bullish's second-quarter results. 
The non-trading category includes lending and liquidity services, interest income, and CoinDesk's data, indices, media and events businesses.
Source: Bullish Q3 2026 results
Lower Advertising Costs Lift Adjusted EBITDA 
The improvement in adjusted EBITDA came as advertising and promotion spending fell to $11.8 million from $22.9 million in the previous quarter. 
Employee compensation also declined, from $29 million to $26.3 million, while headcount remained broadly unchanged at 389 employees compared with 394.
Bullish also revised its full-year outlook, lowering the upper end of its subscriptions and services revenue guidance from $245 million to $235 million. 
The company raised its projected finance expenses to $60–65 million from $52–60 million, while reducing its adjusted operating expense forecast to $220–225 million. 
Separately, Bullish authorised a share repurchase programme of up to $300 million. Though the company is not committed to buying any particular amount of stock and may be suspended or discontinued..


This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.
fullContent:
Bullish reported $576.3 million in third-quarter net income, including a $598.4 million gain from revaluing its digital assets. However, nearly all of the result came from balance-sheet accounting rather than core exchange growth.

The cryptocurrency exchange and information services group reported net income of $18.5 million a year earlier. For the latest quarter, diluted earnings per share reached $3.57, compared with $0.12 on an adjusted basis.

Adjusted net income was $18.7 million, while trading volumes and both major revenue streams declined from the previous quarter. Despite the quarterly profit, Bullish recorded a net loss of $308.6 million for the first nine months of 2026.

Trading and Non-Trading Revenue Decline

Bullish's trading volume and both major revenue streams declined from the second quarter, while lower operating expenses helped lift adjusted EBITDA.

Subscriptions, services and other revenue remained roughly twice adjusted transaction revenue, continuing the pattern Finance Magnates reported after Bullish's second-quarter results.

The non-trading category includes lending and liquidity services, interest income, and CoinDesk's data, indices, media and events businesses.

Source: Bullish Q3 2026 results

Lower Advertising Costs Lift Adjusted EBITDA

The improvement in adjusted EBITDA came as advertising and promotion spending fell to $11.8 million from $22.9 million in the previous quarter.

Employee compensation also declined, from $29 million to $26.3 million, while headcount remained broadly unchanged at 389 employees compared with 394.

Bullish also revised its full-year outlook, lowering the upper end of its subscriptions and services revenue guidance from $245 million to $235 million.

The company raised its projected finance expenses to $60–65 million from $52–60 million, while reducing its adjusted operating expense forecast to $220–225 million.

Separately, Bullish authorised a share repurchase programme of up to $300 million. Though the company is not committed to buying any particular amount of stock and may be suspended or discontinued..

This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.

Traders can access these markets through a single simulated account, with one-step evaluations starting at a one-time fee of $19 for a $1,500 account. The platform combines crypto perpetual futures, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, with xStocks instruments tracking companies such as Apple, NVIDIA and Tesla, alongside stock-index ETFs. Perpetual futures are contracts without an expiry date; xStocks track the prices of underlying shares or ETFs. Positions across the markets share the same account balance and count toward the same evaluation. title: Investment Scams Cost Americans $27,500,000 in Eight Months, Topping Online Purchase Fraud

The post Investment Scams Cost Americans $27,500,000 in Eight Months, Topping Online Purchase Fraud appeared first on The Daily Hodl.
fullContent:
Investment scams have cost Americans $27.5 million in reported losses over eight months, more than any other fraud type that commonly targets older adults.

Homewatch CareGivers says it analyzed Better Business Bureau Scam Tracker reports from January 1st to August 24th.

Online purchase fraud was the most reported scam, with 53,934 reports and $25 million in losses.

Phishing was second by volume, with 27,389 reports and $9 million in losses.

Investment scams ranked lower in volume, with 1,110 reports. Even so, their losses were the highest of any category in the study at $27.5 million.

“Although Online Purchase fraud and Phishing are the most commonly reported scams targeting seniors, Investment scams cost Americans more money. The Better Business Bureau tracked 1,110 Investment scams in our data period, and there were 15 types of scams that were more prevalent than this. But because of the high figures involved in investment scams, the total reported loss equals $27.5 million — three times the cost of Phishing to scam victims and dozens of times the cost of most other fraud types.”

Las Vegas had the highest rate of scams that commonly target seniors among 25 major cities, at 97 per 100,000 residents over an eight-month period.

Victims in Houston lost $1,009,000 to investment fraud, representing 9% of the total losses in the fraud category in Texas.

New Hampshire had the highest rate among states, with 816 reports, or 58 per 100,000 residents.

The figures include reports from victims of all ages, not just seniors.

The post Arthur Hayes Says Anthropic IPO Could Trigger Bitcoin Rally: Do the Numbers Agree? appeared first on 99Bitcoins.
fullContent:
Bitcoin (BTC USD) trades near $64,000 on Wednesday, November 18, the day before Anthropic’s shares start trading on Nasdaq, and BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes says the listing will set Bitcoin’s direction. If the Anthropic IPO pops, Hayes told the New Era Finance Podcast, “it’s game back on. It’s long everything. Risk on.” He added: “Bitcoin’s going to go up too.”

It’s a clean, testable call. So we tested it against the last 12 big IPOs. When a listing jumped 20% or more on its first day, BTC USD was up a median 2% a month later. When it didn’t, Bitcoin was up a median 12%.

Bitcoin needs a lift. It is down 13% in a week, and the Fear & Greed Index, a daily sentiment gauge from 0 to 100, sits at 11, deep in “extreme fear.”

So does an Anthropic pop really mean a Bitcoin rally?

BTC USD After 12 Big IPOs: The Pops Didn’t Pay

We took 12 large listings since 2019, from Uber to SpaceX. For each one, we compared the stock’s first-day close with its IPO price, then measured Bitcoin from the listing day to 7 and 30 days later, using Binance’s daily closes.

  • Big pops: six IPOs jumped 20% or more on day one: Figma, Circle, Airbnb, Snowflake, Rivian and Arm. A week later, Bitcoin was up after four of them, but only by a median 0.9%. A month later, the median was 2%.
  • Small or no pops: after the other six, Bitcoin was up 30 days later five times, with a median gain of 12%. Uber fell 8% on its first day in 2019, and Bitcoin rose 20% over the next month.
  • The closest case: SpaceX gained 19% on its first day in June. BTC USD was flat a week later and flat a month later.

Twelve listings is a small sample, and the market around each one mattered more than the stock. Airbnb’s +120% month came in the December 2020 bull run, and Rivian’s −27% month came at the November 2021 top. What the numbers don’t show is a link between a hot debut and a Bitcoin rally.

DISCOVER: Bitcoin Below Its 200-Week Average for the First Time Since 2022: Is a Drop to $50K Coming or a Historic Buying Opportunity?

Hayes Sees Anthropic as a Test of Risk Appetite

Hayes’s point is less about Anthropic than about mood. A strong debut for the largest AI listing would show that investors are willing to buy risk again, and Bitcoin usually trades as a risk asset. On November 11, he wrote on X that he was adding crypto exposure ahead of the listing, while keeping his positions small enough to exit quickly.

Demand for the shares looks strong. Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 a share in its roadshow announcement. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that demand could push the price above $80. On Hyperliquid, a crypto exchange, a pre-IPO contract on the shares trades about 24% above that.

The other side is money. At the top of the range, the listing raises about $64 billion. Some of that cash comes from investors selling other assets, and Bitcoin slid about 20% in the weeks before SpaceX’s record listing in June.

DISCOVER: Top 20 Crypto to Buy in 2026

BTC USD Price Analysis: $65,500 Is the First Test

On the daily chart, BTC USD trades at $64,069. That is below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $75,755, and its 200-day EMA at $75,753.

  • Resistance: $65,500, a level Bitcoin bounced from in February, March and April and was turned back from in June, July and August. Above that, $74,300, which capped prices in March and held as a floor in April, May and September.
  • Support: $62,300, Sunday’s low. Bitcoin bounced near it in February, June, July and August. Below it, $57,800, the July low and the bottom of the past year.
Path What has to happen Next stop
Bullish A strong Anthropic debut and a daily close above $65,500 $74,300, the March-September level
Sideways A modest debut, price between $62,300 and $65,500 A range near current levels
Bearish A weak debut or a daily close below $62,300 $57,800, the July low

Hayes may still be right about the mood. But if history is a guide, a big Anthropic pop is not enough on its own. BTC USD needs buyers to come back to crypto, not just to AI stocks.

fullContent:
Oracle released its November edition of Critical Security Patch Update. The update received patches for 655 security vulnerabilities. Some of the vulnerabilities addressed in this update impact more than one product. These patches address vulnerabilities in various product families, including third-party components in Oracle products.

Out of the 655 security updates published, a total of 62 (9.5%) vulnerabilities are rated critical, 249 are rated as important (38%), and 274 are rated as medium.

In this Oracle Critical Security Patch Update, Oracle Hyperion received the highest number of patches, 267, constituting about 41% of the total patches released.

71 of the 655 (about 11%) security patches provided by the November Critical Security Patch Update are for non-Oracle CVEs, such as open-source components included in and exploitable within Oracle product distributions.

This batch of security patches received 20 updates for Oracle Database products. The following is the product-wise distribution: 

  • 7 new security updates for Oracle Database Server with a maximum reported CVSS Base Score of 9.9.
    • None of these updates applies to client-only deployments of the Oracle Database.
  • 2 new security updates for Oracle APEX with a maximum reported CVSS Base Score of 9.8.
  • 3 new security updates for Oracle Autonomous Health Framework with a maximum reported CVSS Base Score of 9.1.
  • 8 new security updates for Oracle REST Data Services with a maximum reported CVSS Base Score of 9.8.

The complete list of Oracle product families and the no of patches issued are listed below:

Qualys QID Coverage

Qualys has released the following QIDs mentioned in the table:

Note: The table will be updated with additional QIDs once released.

Notable Oracle Vulnerabilities Patched

Oracle Hyperion

This Critical Security Patch Update for Oracle Hyperion received 267 security patches. Out of these, 107 vulnerabilities can be exploited over a network without user credentials.

A total of 12 vulnerabilities have critical severity ratings.

Oracle Supply Chain

This Critical Security Patch Update for Oracle Supply Chain received 74 security patches. Out of these, 36 vulnerabilities can be exploited over a network without user credentials.

CVE-2026-114980, CVE-2026-127324, CVE-2026-127325, CVE-2026-127326, CVE-2026-127327, and CVE-2026-101356 have critical severity ratings.

Oracle E-Business Suite

This Critical Security Patch Update for Oracle E-Business Suite received 71 security patches. Out of these, 19 vulnerabilities can be exploited over a network without user credentials.

CVE-2026-114880, CVE-2026-114924, CVE-2026-114925, CVE-2026-114863, CVE-2026-101691, and CVE-2026-114881 have critical severity ratings.

Oracle Fusion Middleware

This Critical Security Patch Update for Oracle Fusion Middleware received 71 security patches. Out of these, 19 vulnerabilities can be exploited over a network without user credentials.

CVE-2026-114880, CVE-2026-114924, CVE-2026-114925, CVE-2026-114863, CVE-2026-101691, and CVE-2026-114881 have critical severity ratings.

Oracle Communications

This Critical Security Patch Update for Oracle Communications received 31 security patches. Out of these, 21 vulnerabilities can be exploited over a network without user credentials.

CVE-2026-111497, CVE-2026-1229, CVE-2026-41889, and CVE-2026-114820 have critical severity ratings.

title: NEAR Price Squeezed Into a 29-Cent Range by Three Levels
description:
Summary Price sits just above the 0.618 retracement. The 100-day SMA near $3.52 caps rebounds. Candles are testing the channel’s […]
The post NEAR Price Squeezed Into a 29-Cent Range by Three Levels appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Summary

  • Price sits just above the 0.618 retracement.
  • The 100-day SMA near $3.52 caps rebounds.
  • Candles are testing the channel’s upper edge.
  • Moving-average order still favors the longer trend.

On the daily NEAR/USDT chart from Binance, the token trades at $3.34, down 1.59% on the day after opening at $3.40 and moving between $3.31 and $3.43.

Where the reference points come from

Every level that matters here traces back to one move. NEAR bottomed near $1.52 in August and ran to a high close to $5.99 by mid-October, nearly quadrupling in about two months.

Stretch a Fibonacci grid over that rally and the map fills in. The 0.236 sits near $4.93, the 0.382 around $4.28 and the 0.5 near $3.76. Lower down, the 0.618 lands close to $3.23, with the 0.786 around $2.48.

The top took weeks to form. Through late September and most of October, NEAR chopped between the 0.382 area and levels above the 0.236, tagging its high near $6 along the way. It was a grind, not a spike and a crash.

A channel of lower highs

Then the selling got organized and from late October, price slid inside a descending parallel channel, with each bounce peaking below the last one and each low undercutting the one before it.

Volume never screamed panic. The decline inside the channel came without a capitulation-sized spike, and today’s 9.37 million NEAR is moderate. This was steady selling, not a forced flush.

Mid-November brought the real stress test. NEAR slipped below the 0.618, then climbed back over it within days. Traders watch that line closely. It’s the deepest standard retracement that still reads as a pullback inside a bigger advance, and past it only the 0.786 stands between price and losing most of the rally.

Three levels inside 29 cents

The bounce off the 0.618 ran straight into the channel’s upper boundary. The last two sessions sit on that line or just above it. Today’s small red candle shows sellers defending it.

Just overhead waits the 100-day SMA at $3.52, the first ceiling for any rebound. So the squeeze is tight. The 0.618 sits underneath, the 100 SMA above, and the channel line cuts right through the current candles, all within a $0.29 range.

One session poking over a trendline isn’t a breakout. A run of daily closes clearly outside the channel would be. Closes above the 100 SMA would make that case far harder to argue with.

READ MORE:

Why a 5% Stablecoin Return Can Still Cost Holders Money

Bent trend, not a broken one

The 50-day SMA carries the bearish half of the story. At about $4.42, it has rolled over and now slopes down, well above price. That’s the plainest evidence that the medium-term trend has turned against buyers.

Further down, the picture changes. The 200-day SMA at $2.72 is still rising. And the averages haven’t crossed: the 50 still sits above the 100, which still sits above the 200. A bearish crossover would mean a shorter average dropping under a longer one, and none has happened yet. The structure built during the rally is dented, not dismantled.

Momentum backs that read. The 14-day RSI prints 39.65, under the 50 midline, so sellers keep the edge for now. Yet it has hooked higher and sits above its own moving average at 37.02. Through the whole decline, it stayed above the oversold line at 30.

Beyond each edge of the band

Either side can give way first. Here’s what the chart has waiting.

Break above $3.52

A daily close over the 100 SMA, with price outside the channel, brings the 0.5 near $3.76 into view. Past that, the 0.382 around $4.28 and the falling 50 SMA at $4.42 stack into a thicker resistance zone.

Slip below $3.23

If sellers reject the channel top and price loses the 0.618 near $3.23, the rising 200 SMA at $2.72 is the first level in the way. The 0.786 around $2.48 sits beneath it.

What decides the label: neither path is a forecast. As long as NEAR holds the 0.618 and the 200 SMA keeps climbing, the drop from $5.99 still reads as a deep correction of the $1.52 rally. A sustained move below both would turn it into a broken trend.

The first signal won’t be dramatic. It’s a run of daily closes clearly above the channel line, not one candle. If those closes arrive with the RSI back over 50, buyers would hold the momentum edge as well as the structure. Until then, the channel still sets the terms.

fullContent:
WASHINGTON—Claiming that such monitoring efforts had been a waste of government resources, Federal Bureau of Investigation officials announced Friday that the agency would discontinue its longstanding practice of tracking serial killers.

Though the FBI’s Violent Criminal Apprehension Program has historically enjoyed bipartisan approval for its role in the capture of murderers like the Golden State Killer and Samuel Little, the bureau has come under scrutiny in recent months amid the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to downsize federal agencies. Director Kash Patel has repeatedly argued that Americans should stop expecting the government to hunt down every serial killer who binds and gags victims before tossing their bodies in the trunk of a car. 

“Today we are ending the senseless and inefficient tracking of America’s homicidal maniacs,” said Patel, who stated that the decision to no longer collect information related to serial killers was driven primarily by the high costs associated with processing DNA evidence, identifying human remains, and prosecuting federal murder charges. “The fact is, if a crazed necrophile is chasing you through the woods with a pair of hedge shears, it’s not the taxpayers’ job to bail you out. Those kinds of handouts might have flown with the socialist Biden FBI, but not anymore.”

“Our common-sense position is that these depraved, gratification-seeking murderers aren’t the government’s problem,” Patel added.

Despite Patel’s dismissive attitude toward murders and bloody, violent crime scenes, some experts have voiced concerns that ending federal investigations of active killers such as the San Diego Strangler and the Alabama Ripper could allow rates of serial homicides to rebound to levels not seen since the 1970s. According to reports, the FBI has ceased to archive dozens of human fingers mailed to them by uncaptured serial killers and has sold off its forensics laboratory at Quantico to a Trump-linked condominium developer. Critics argue this move could leave the bureau without the institutional capacity to hunt down any violent psychopaths obsessed with constructing a suit out of human skin who may arise in the future.

Despite these criticisms, a number of Americans expressed concerns about government overreach infringing on the civil liberties of anyone who kills for their own personal pleasure and gratification. 

“I don’t know why these woke liberals are so afraid of serial killers,” said Idaho resident Mike Howe, who noted that there were millions of acres of forest where the decapitated remains of victims were buried and claimed that it was “none of our business.” “There’s things we can do without spending millions of dollars to track down every single mentally unstable auto mechanic targeting brunette women who resemble his domineering mother.”

While the decision to curtail federal investigation of serial killers so far appears to have garnered widespread disapproval from law enforcement agencies and public safety groups, the policy shift nevertheless has its staunch defenders.

 “I get why some people are opposed to this change, but I’m glad the Trump administration is letting me collect more slaves to serve me in the afterlife,” said the Ouroboros Killer, an as-of-yet unidentified murderer who has repeatedly voiced his support for the FBI’s actions in numerous cryptographic ciphers mailed to news-
papers across the country. “It feels so good when I slide that knife in, but even better is when the president takes a knife to wasteful government spending.”

 “Government efficiency is the ultimate thrill,” the Ouroboros continued. “I am not afraid of death because I know that in paradise all the tax dollars Trump has saved by slashing government bloat will be waiting for me. Ouroboros = 31, inefficient federal bureaucracy = 0.”

title: The Chopping Block: Crypto's Brutal Week With FalconX's Josh Lim, CZ vs. Star, the Anthropic IPO, and Should Jensen Huang Come Back?
description:
Welcome to The Chopping Block, where crypto insiders Haseeb Qureshi, Tom Schmidt, Tarun Chitra, and Robert Leshner chop it up about the latest in crypto. This week they are joined by Joshua Lim, Global Co-Head of Markets at FalconX.

Six red weeks in a row, BTC down to 65K, the fear and greed index at 10, and a $20 billion contraction in stablecoins. Josh walks through what his desk saw: a hidden buildup in leverage, end-of-year hedges in IBIT puts, and a weekend sell-off concentrated on Coinbase. The hosts react to the Situational Awareness 13F coming out down 92%, and Haseeb calls it the Multicoin of AI. Josh says the numbers don't support Star's claim that Binance is dumping on the market, and Haseeb explains how far back the CZ and Star feud goes. Then the Anthropic IPO: Tarun asks whether a flop would actually be better for crypto, Haseeb bets newly liquid Anthropic employees buy crypto, and Robert says Anthropic's unlock schedules are bringing the weirdness back. Tom asks what crypto's next catalyst is, and Haseeb and Tarun argue over whether past bear markets ever had a narrative. They close on Jensen Huang's exit from NVIDIA: Robert says he crossed a major line, Tarun makes the case that he willed NVIDIA into existence, and Haseeb says tech is misreading the moment.

title: Etherscan Warns of Support System Access Attempts as Security Scares Hit Crypto and Banks
description:
Etherscan warns of attempts to access its support systems as Freshworks, Optimizely and major banking security incidents raise questions about crypto and traditional finance security.
The post Etherscan Warns of Support System Access Attempts as Security Scares Hit Crypto and Banks appeared first on Cryptonews.
fullContent:
Another day, another security scare. This time, Etherscan is warning users after detecting attempts to gain unauthorized access to its customer support system. But the timing could hardly be worse for an industry already dealing with a growing list of cyberattacks.

The warning comes just days after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, injecting malicious code into websites operated by 178 organizations. The affected names included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, and CNN.

Meanwhile, crypto platforms have faced separate attacks involving compromised API keys, protocol vulnerabilities, and stolen customer information. Traditional banking has not escaped either, with a French bank recently losing approximately €100 million to hackers.

So what kind of security era are we entering? The problem is no longer confined to crypto exchanges or experimental DeFi protocols. Banks, technology companies, payment providers and blockchain businesses are increasingly exposed to the same interconnected digital infrastructure.

Discover: The Best Token Presales

Etherscan, Optimizely and 178 Websites Hacked: Nobody Seems Safe

Etherscan disclosed earlier today that attackers had attempted to gain unauthorized access to its Freshworks customer support and ticketing system. The company is investigating and has introduced precautionary measures. It has not confirmed that customer records were successfully accessed, but warned users about suspicious support communications, unexpected links, and requests for sensitive information.

The concern is particularly relevant because support impersonation remains an effective way to steal users’ crypto and money. An attacker posing as an Etherscan representative could exploit a user’s existing support request to make a phishing message appear legitimate.

But Etherscan is hardly the only name facing security questions this week. Just two days ago, hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation signup process. They injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects, allowing the code to run on websites using the affected software.

Security researchers identified 178 organizations whose websites carried the malicious code. The list included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, Zoom, Salesforce, CNN and Equifax. The injected script attempted to replace crypto wallet addresses with attacker-controlled alternatives. It also targeted payment-card information, cookies and screenshots, while attempting to deliver exploit code against older iPhones.

Optimizely confirmed the vulnerability and said it had removed the injected code and fixed the flaw. Its November 17 incident report said the unauthorized party exploited the signup process rather than stealing customer administrator passwords.

The financial damage remains unclear. It is reported that investigators could not establish how many visitors were affected or whether the attempted thefts succeeded.

The uncomfortable takeaway is that attackers did not need to breach 178 separate companies. They exploited one software provider whose code was embedded across hundreds of websites.

Crypto Exchanges and Banks Are Both Taking Hits

Crypto’s security problems extend beyond Etherscan and the Optimizely incident. DeFiLlama’s hack tracker recorded several attacks during the week, including a $10.39 million incident involving Lighter Perps on November 16. The attacker exploited a compromised trader API key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

Lighter said its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. It temporarily suspended withdrawals and activated Guardian mode to prevent further unauthorized activity.

Another incident hit MORE Markets, where an attacker exploited a lending mechanism to drain approximately $308,000 in WFLOW. B18 TimeBank also suffered an exploit on November 17, losing $404,540 in USDC through its reward voucher redemption mechanism.

These incidents show different weaknesses across crypto infrastructure. Not every loss comes from a broken smart contract. Compromised credentials, vulnerable applications and flawed authorization mechanisms can be equally damaging.

Traditional finance faces its own problems. French lender Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed a cyber heist earlier in November, with hackers stealing approximately €100 million through fraudulent transactions originating from the bank’s own accounts. The bank said customer assets were not affected, although some transactions were temporarily suspended.

Deutsche Bank also made headlines on November 17 after confidential internal documents surfaced through an international journalistic investigation. It was a document leak, not a confirmed breach of its current banking systems.

Deutsche Bank said security testing found no indication that its current IT environment, account information, login credentials, or payment data had been compromised. Still, the leak could have wider geopolitical repercussions.

Banking institutions are not immune to major security incidents simply because they operate under traditional financial regulations.

Is Crypto Actually Less Safe Than Traditional Banking?

Crypto has suffered enormous losses. The October Binance incident alone involved $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, making it one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Yet, traditional finance also faces attacks involving payment infrastructure, third-party service providers, and internal transaction systems.

The Optimizely incident is particularly revealing. Both HSBC and Ledger appeared among the affected organizations. The vulnerability did not care whether visitors were interacting with a traditional financial institution or a crypto company.

Neither system offers complete protection. The real question is whether companies can secure the increasingly complex infrastructure connecting their services. A single compromised vendor can expose hundreds of organizations, while one stolen credential can bypass otherwise sophisticated security systems.

Crypto users have every reason to demand stronger protections. But traditional banking customers should not mistake regulation and familiar branding for immunity.

With Etherscan investigating attempted unauthorized access, the data provider is now joining the growing list of companies dealing with security incidents.

title: Cognizant and Qualys Redefine AI-Era Managed Security Service
description: Cognizant will use the full Qualys portfolio to bring its clients what the frontier AI era demands: AI-speed detection, hyper-prioritization, and confident remediation for every zero-day. When a critical zero-day goes public, security leaders ask two questions: which assets are affected, and how fast can we safely fix them? For most enterprises, the current answer […]
fullContent:
Cognizant will use the full Qualys portfolio to bring its clients what the frontier AI era demands: AI-speed detection, hyper-prioritization, and confident remediation for every zero-day.

When a critical zero-day goes public, security leaders ask two questions: which assets are affected, and how fast can we safely fix them? For most enterprises, the current answer is days, then weeks.

Frontier AI makes that remediation timeframe dangerous. Microsoft’s November Patch Tuesday alone carried 1,093 vulnerabilities, up from 93 in November 2025 before frontier AI models arrived. AI-assisted attackers can weaponize a new advisory in four to twelve hours, while scan-driven detection often takes 24 to 36 hours just to show which assets are affected. The risk is already real: Cognizant’s 2026 Cybersecurity Pulse Poll found that 83% of participating U.S. enterprises had an AI-related security incident in the past 24 months.

Knowing what to fix is only half the gap. Every step from finding to fix is still gated by people, for one reason: fear that a patch will break production, that a reboot will take down a critical system, or that there is no fast way back. Teams will not hand fixes to automation they do not trust.

Cognizant helps the world’s largest enterprises scale with AI, through its AI Builder approach, and recognizes that its clients need security that moves at machine speed. Already running managed services on Qualys ETM, Cognizant is now expanding to the full Qualys portfolio, including TruRisk Eliminate. That is why I am excited to welcome Cognizant to the Qualys Global mROC Alliance.

Managed detection is table stakes. This is the dawn of the 24-hour autonomous remediation service, run from Qualys ETM: a zero-day disclosed, detected, prioritized, and remediated within a day.

Why the Qualys Platform Fits Cognizant’s Approach

Running zero-day response as a service, at enterprise scale, puts specific demands on the platform underneath. Cognizant needed three capabilities working as one:

  • One record for every asset, across every tool, built from Qualys and non-Qualys sources, so there is no reconciling data across disparate tools before anyone can act.
  • Exploit validation in each client’s own environment, so every hour of the client’s team’s time goes to risk that is real.
  • Remediation with confidence, so automation can be trusted within production systems.

Qualys delivers all three on one platform, with the agentic AI to run them at machine speed.

Cognizant brings what a platform alone cannot: Cyber Vulnerability Management services and threat intelligence, delivery experience inside large enterprises, and a view of risk in financial terms for the board. Its operators run the Risk Operations Center, powered by Qualys ETM to navigate inside each client’s own tools, change windows, and approvals. Clients keep control of what gets fixed and when. Cognizant carries the daily work.

“Our 2026 Cybersecurity Pulse Poll shows that strength in one control, such as detection or remediation, still leaves enterprises exposed in the AI era. Together with Qualys, we are connecting detection, prioritization and remediation into one managed operating model, helping clients reduce risk, strengthen resilience and scale AI with confidence.”
— Vishal Salvi, SVP and Global Head of Cybersecurity, Cognizant

Cognizant will deliver four mROC services on the Qualys platform:

  • Cyber risk quantification and advisory services. Cyber risk for business applications shown in dollars, with a personalized risk plan and a report for the board.
  • Onboarding and integration. The security tools a customer already owns connected into one record for each asset, with data quality checked from day one.
  • Risk monitoring as a managed service. AI-speed alerts on new CVEs, a validated queue instead of noise, and a weekly exposure review, using InstaScan, Agent Val, and ROCky.

Risk remediation as a managed service. A wave-based plan built from the Risk Elimination Playbook, zero-touch remediation where it is safe, and proof the fix held, using TruRisk Eliminate, TruConfidence, and Agent Sara.

AI-Speed Detection: Every Exposure Known in Minutes

Frontier AI has changed the rhythm of disclosure. Vulnerabilities now land in volume, and attackers act on them in hours, well inside any scan cycle.

Qualys InstaScan, delivered by Agent Insta, closes that gap. It turns the inventory and telemetry a client already has, from Qualys and non-Qualys sources, into high-confidence findings within minutes of disclosure. No new scan, no new agent.

On November’s Patch Tuesday, InstaScan delivered 90% of detections within minutes. The first landed about 40 minutes before Microsoft’s own release notes went live. With Cognizant, that speed turns into action. Through its risk monitoring service, Cognizant analysts watch for new disclosures every day, confirm each exposure, and route it to the right asset owner with context. The client’s team no longer chases owners or rebuilds asset lists every time a new CVE trends.

Hyper-Prioritization: Proven Exploitability

More vulnerabilities do not mean more risk. Of the 48,172 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2025, the Qualys Threat Research Unit found only 357 (0.74%) confirmed remotely exploitable and actively weaponized. No team can work the full list, and none should have to.

Agent Val and TruConfirm test what is actually exploitable in the client’s own environment, with existing controls counted. Critical on paper but blocked by a control? It leaves the urgent queue. Exploitable on a PCI-scoped server? It goes to the top.

Cyber Risk Quantification (CRQ) then puts validated risk in dollars, by business application, so the CISO can show the board what each fix is worth.

With Cognizant, the short list becomes a working rhythm. Through its risk monitoring and advisory services, Cognizant keeps each client’s validated queue current and reviews it with them every week. The client’s team stops triaging noise and starts each week knowing exactly what to fix first.

Autonomous Remediation: Remediate with Confidence and Maintain Operational Resiliency

That fear is why the global mean time to remediate sits at about 30 days. TruRisk Eliminate, with TruConfidence, removes it by protecting operational resiliency before, during, and after every change.

  • Before: TruRisk Eliminate chooses the safest fix for each finding: patch, mitigate, isolate, or uninstall. A patch reliability score decides what deploys automatically and what goes ring by ring.
  • During: Changes roll out in waves, starting with low-risk rings. System health is watched through each wave, and rollback restores a known-good state if health drops.
  • After: AI-powered patch failure analysis pinpoints why a change failed and the corrective actions, and automated rollback restores a known-good state.

Showing clients the 1% that matters

Cognizant can open every client engagement with a Risk Elimination Playbook, powered by TruConfidence and built for that client’s environment. It narrows the backlog to the 1% that must be fixed now and moves the rest into planned software updates. It also benchmarks the client’s mean time to remediate against peers, and shows how much of the backlog autonomous remediation can close, and how much faster.

It becomes the plan behind every remediation wave and the baseline for every review.

Where Managed Security Goes Next

The three pillars together provide a new kind of service: 24-hour autonomous remediation, run from ETM. Cognizant can take a critical zero-day from disclosure to remediation within a day, for every client, with operational resiliency built in at every step.

Managed security is moving from raising alerts to closing risk. Cognizant is among the first to deliver that at enterprise scale, and I expect it to set the bar enterprises hold every provider to. That is what the Global mROC Alliance was built for: the platform, the certification path, and the operating model to run the Risk Operations Center as a service.

Attackers already move at AI speed. This expanded partnership helps tip the balance back toward the defense.

To learn more, visit the Qualys Global mROC Alliance page, read the press release, or contact your Cognizant or Qualys account team.

fullContent:
A newly emerged ransomware gang has listed Visa and JPMorgan Chase as alleged victims and threatens to leak stolen data within 48 hours.

The gang, which goes by the name n0n, has given the two companies 48 hours to negotiate, reports Cybernews.

Visa says it is aware of the claims and that the incident involved a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region.

Says a Visa spokesperson,

“Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. There is no indication that payment data such as card numbers have been affected.”

Visa has not said which third-party service providers were hit.

Meanwhile, JPMorgan Chase is separately dealing with a service outage that it blames on a software bug.

The bank says there is “no evidence” linking the disruption to a cyberattack.

The bank has not said whether the outage has any connection to the gang’s claims.

The n0n gang was first tracked in mid-September.

The gang claimed last week that it stole billions of traveler records from Expedia.

The attackers have offered few details about what they claim to have stolen from Visa and JPMorgan Chase.

The Daily HODL previously reported that JPMorgan Chase and other major US banks suffered a major outage that involved login failures and missing account balances.

Trump is trying to put the Iran war behind him, but it's not over
description:
MANAMA, Bahrain - President Donald Trump appears eager to put the unpopular war with Iran behind him, as Democrats prepare to assume the majority on Capitol Hill after Republicans’ staggering midterm losses.
But there is no indication that the war Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu started is anywhere near finished. The major issues of the conflict - control of the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. naval blockade, the fate of Iran’s nuclear program, Tehran’s support for regional proxies - remain unresolved. And Tehran’s perception of waning U.S. political will has left it emboldened. 
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. 
Over the past week - following remarks by Trump at Arlington National Cemetery in which he said the war had been “won” - Iran three times has targeted the small nation of Bahrain, home to a massive U.S. naval base, with drones. On Wednesday it said it targeted a military base in Kuwait that is also home to U.S. forces in a drone and missile attack.
The renewed Iranian strikes on Persian Gulf countries, the first in months, come as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels hit Saudi Arabia, and on top of severe economic damage wrought by Iran’s attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.
In the strait, a vital waterway for the region’s oil shipments, videos verified by The Washington Post show tankers on fire and plumes of smoke billowing amid daily attacks this month. 
Iranian leaders, riding high on what they see as the U.S. voters’ rebuke of Trump in the midterms, show little sign of backing down. 
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament, warned in a speech on Sunday that the status quo of international economic pressure, which Trump has embraced as a key strategy to force eventual capitulation, is not sustainable. While Iran is open to negotiations if the United States accepts its demands, he said, Iran’s military “will determine the geography of the battlefield” if the U.S. “makes another mistake.” 
Both Iran and the U.S. “are scared of being seen as weak, and so they don’t want to make the first concession” in negotiations, said Abdulla Banndar Al-Etaibi, an assistant professor of international affairs at Qatar University. 
The two sides are so unpredictable, he said, that “anything is possible” in terms of escalation. 
“How can this be considered anything other than a victory for Iran?” asked Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, a Washington think tank.
“The regime is surviving. The nuclear program is damaged but will be reconstituted, and they have realized what a jewel they have in terms of the Strait of Hormuz,” Vatanka said. “They will hold Gulf states hostage for years to come.” 
In response to requests for comment about ongoing violence in Hormuz and the resulting economic costs, the White House said in a statement that Iran is a “failed country” and  that the U.S. “is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing.” 
Trump has said that a combination of a U.S. naval blockade and sanctions are crushing Iran’s economy and will force Iran to make a deal. The Trump administration has claimed that a massive U.S. military operation protecting vessels shuttling oil from the Persian Gulf into the Gulf of Oman, which launched in August, has helped get oil flows to prewar levels.
But in the first 16 days of November, there were 16 attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy - following a record high of 37 attacks in October. In one of the most dramatic videos, posted on social media Nov. 8  and verified by The Post, a massive red Navig8 tanker is seen in flames near the coast of Oman as another boat sprays water on it.  
Satellite imagery captured by the European Space Agency satellite Sentinel-2  of the site of the attack shows a plume of smoke so large that it touches the shore. Oil spilled from damaged tankers has reached the shores of the United Arab Emirates and Oman, according to local media reports. 
Iranian state media has also reported that at least eight ships struck mines last week and over the weekend while traveling in waters that Iran considers restricted. U.S. Central Command posted a video Nov. 7 showing it firing “multiple precision munitions” at a commercial ship traveling in the Gulf of Oman that it said ignored U.S. warnings. 
The price of oil is down from record highs as the market has priced in the risk of travel through the strait, said Gregory Brew, a Middle East energy analyst with the consultancy Eurasia Group. But prices are still dramatically higher than before the war, he added, and overall traffic through the strait is a fraction of what it was before the war. 
“The Strait of Hormuz is neither open nor closed - it is contested,” Brew said. “The U.S. leaning back does not mean the war ends, especially for the Gulf.” 
The war has left the region mired in simmering conflict with no clear path to a decisive military outcome or broad peace agreement.
In the early weeks of the war, when Iranian drones and missiles rained down on the Gulf, hitting hotels in Dubai, the U.S. military base in Bahrain and Qatar’s liquefied natural gas plant, Gulf officials publicly doubled down on their partnerships with the United States.
Privately, many in the region bemoaned Trump’s decision to go to war and wondered whether the region would be left to pick up the pieces when he grew tired of the war they had warned him not to start. 
Nearly nine months in, with Trump saying the diplomatic solution sought by Qatar and backed by the rest of the Gulf is unnecessary, there is a sense of resignation. No one wants to publicly criticize Trump - the U.S. is still the Gulf’s main security guarantor - but speeches by top officials these days focus more on regional cooperation and expanding partnerships than the U.S. relationship.
In interviews in recent weeks in Qatar, Bahrain and the UAE, residents said they felt both whiplash and a sense of hopelessness. 
Across the wealthy Gulf, nations have taken economic hits because of the war: The International Monetary Fund projects that gross domestic product will have contracted by an average of nearly 5 percent this year. 
But impact has been uneven, and most dramatically felt in Bahrain, Qatar and Kuwait, which do not have ports or any other viable options to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
In Qatar, which has long ranked as one of the world’s wealthiest countries by GDP per capita, state revenue dropped in the first half of the year by 42 percent, Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said last month. But the impact on everyday life has been limited, residents said. 
In Bahrain, an import-reliant island nation of 1.6 million that has far less oil and gas wealth than others in the region, the impact has been more acute. The country has seen its economy devastated by continued turmoil in Hormuz. 
Around the capital Manama on a recent day, storefront after storefront was shuttered, “for rent” signs in the windows. 
A supermarket manager said residents are only filling half their carts because of price hikes. Hair stylists said that their salon, empty on a recent Thursday afternoon, would have been bustling before the war. 
“I am nervous all the time,” said an artist. A steep drop in tourism forced him to close his shop. “It is the whole world that is suffering.”
“We just want the U.S. to stop interfering,” said the artist, speaking on the condition of anonymity because of concerns about criticizing the U.S., a Bahraini ally. 
Sirens rang out across the country Sunday morning and again on Tuesday, as  Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said its drones were targeting U.S. military equipment. The government once again warned residents to seek shelter. 
Bahrain’s media office said in a statement that the country had been “subjected to repeated and unjustifiable Iranian attacks on its territory.” 
As the sun set and a group of men prepared to head to the mosque for evening prayers, they bemoaned the situation. Abdul Aziz said that he used to make a living importing motorbikes and bicycles that he sold to U.S. soldiers at the naval base in Bahrain. 
Now, he said, goods that used to take a month to arrive are taking four. The Americans he used to sell to are gone - thousands of them evacuated from the base ahead of the war. 
The market, he said, “has died because of the war and because of Hormuz.”
“I don’t know until when we will suffer,” he said. “But we just want things to be normal again.” 
George and Steckelberg reported from Washington, and Piper from London.
         
Related Content
This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/18/trump-is-trying-put-iran-war-behind-him-its-not-over/

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Future of Finance Institute (FFI) outlined an Agentic Money Sandbox on November 18, 2026, at the Singapore FinTech Festival. The testbed lets banks try AI agents that start digital-money payments and treasury moves. Agents must stay inside set authority, limits, and safeguards before any live rollout.

The joint MAS and FFI release ties the sandbox to Singapore’s National AI Missions for financial services. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, who chairs MAS, named the third mission as enabling safe agentic transactions. In his SFF 2026 keynote, he said greater autonomy for agents must come with clear responsibility. Agents work inside set authority and limits. Institutions and enterprises stay accountable for actions taken on their behalf.

What the Agentic Money Sandbox Is Testing

FFI will run the sandbox as a shared lab, not a public retail product. Banks can build and exercise the controls AI agents need to move digital money safely. The release names early use cases as agent-initiated payments and treasury management across participating banks.

The stake is practical. An AI agent can pay a supplier, sweep idle cash, or settle an invoice without a human click on every step. That only helps if the bank can prove who authorized the agent, what it could spend, and who owns the loss if it misfires. The sandbox is where those proofs get stress-tested before live books take the hit.

MAS and FFI also named FFI’s bank launch partners at SFF 2026: DBS, OCBC, Standard Chartered, and UOB. Those banks sit with technology and research partners on the broader National AI Missions programme, not only on the money sandbox.

How Purpose-Bound Limits Are Meant to Constrain Agents

Gan’s keynote put one concrete control path on the table: purpose bound money. In that framing, conditions ride with the funds. An agent can move money only when preset rules are met. His examples are blunt. An agent could pay a contract once the terms have been checked. Or it could finish a purchase for a user inside limits already written into the money.

That is the mechanism in plain order. First the money carries a purpose, a cap, and a permission set. Then the agent checks whether those conditions hold. Then the payment fires. The trials must also examine identity, authority, accountability, and interoperability before wider use.

For AI and blockchain readers, the interesting split is not “AI decides” versus “a human clicks.” It is whether programmable limits on digital money can make an autonomous payment look more like a constrained instruction than an open wallet. Purpose-bound rails are the candidate answer MAS is willing to test. They are not a claim that every Singapore bank deposit is already programmable that way.

Why a Sandbox Matters Before Live Agentic Payments

Agent-led payments change the failure mode. A mistaken human transfer is usually one bad click. A mistaken agent can repeat a bad rule at machine speed across banks. Gan’s speech frames the upside as faster cash management and machine-led commerce. The same speech refuses to detach that upside from accountability under financial regulation.

The sandbox therefore has a dual job. It asks what value agents can create in payments and treasury. It also asks which safeguards must exist before those agents leave the lab. Banks need shared ways to prove identity, grant authority, assign accountability, and work across institutions.

Xinhua independently reported the same Wednesday package. FFI is establishing the Agentic Money Sandbox so banks can test AI agents that conduct digital-money transactions inside defined limits and safeguards. The wire matches the MAS fact pattern. It does not add a go-live date or production volumes.

What Is Demonstrated, and Where the Catch Sits

What the primary record shows today is a named testbed and a policy frame. MAS and FFI announced the Agentic Money Sandbox. Initial cases are agent payments and treasury management. Purpose bound money is an explicit trial area in the chairman’s keynote. Four large banks are listed as FFI launch partners. The sandbox’s stated job is to test controls before live deployment.

What remains unproven is harder and more important. The release does not publish a start date for live agent traffic. It also skips a schedule of which payment rails will sit under the sandbox, and it shows no results from completed agent payment drills. Embedding conditions into money can constrain an agent’s spending. It does not prove the agent’s judgment about a contract, an invoice, or a treasury move was correct. Verification of permission is not verification of good decisions.

The mental model to keep is simple. Singapore is not declaring that AI agents already run the country’s digital payments. It is building a controlled room where banks practice letting agents move digital money under purpose-bound limits, identity checks, and clear accountability. Only then will they decide what is safe to take live.

title: Coinbase Brings ChatGPT Into Crypto Trading as Pancake Rebrand Signals Binance Rivalry
description:
Coinbase brings crypto trading to ChatGPT as Pancake drops Swap from its name, raising the stakes in the race against Binance DeFi ecosystem.
The post Coinbase Brings ChatGPT Into Crypto Trading as Pancake Rebrand Signals Binance Rivalry appeared first on Cryptonews.
fullContent:
Coinbase is bringing crypto trading directly into ChatGPT as competition for AI-powered financial services intensifies. Meanwhile, PancakeSwap has dropped “Swap” from its name, expanding beyond decentralized trading. The two developments show how Coinbase and Binance-linked crypto projects are positioning themselves for the next phase of digital finance.

Coinbase announced its ChatGPT integration yesterday, allowing users to connect accounts and manage portfolios. Users can check balances, analyze holdings, and place eligible trades using everyday language. And every order requires explicit approval before execution.

The timing coincides with Pancake’s attempt to reposition itself beyond its original decentralized exchange business.

Discover: The Best Token Presales

Coinbase Brings Crypto Trading Directly Into ChatGPT

The Coinbase plugin allows eligible users to trade crypto and equities without leaving ChatGPT. Users can request market or limit orders through conversational instructions.

Before execution, ChatGPT displays an interactive confirmation card showing order details. Users must approve the transaction before Coinbase processes it through its Advanced Trade platform. Standard trading fees, eligibility requirements, and account limits still apply.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong described the integration as another step toward an emerging agentic economy. The idea involves AI assistants handling increasingly complex financial tasks for users. But Coinbase still keeps humans responsible for approving individual trades for now.

The integration also builds on Coinbase’s AI infrastructure. Its Coinbase for Agents toolkit provides developers with connections to trading accounts and market data. The ChatGPT launch brings those capabilities into a more accessible consumer interface.

As of today, the official integration currently remains limited to eligible U.S. Coinbase users. It also depends on ChatGPT account and workspace availability.

Pancake Rebrand Takes Binance’s DeFi Ecosystem Beyond Swaps

While Coinbase expands through ChatGPT, Pancake is changing how users perceive its decentralized trading ecosystem. Formerly known as PancakeSwap, the platform announced its rebrand today. The new identity reflects six years of expansion beyond its original token-swapping business.

Pancake now operates across more than 11 blockchain networks. The platform reports over 208 million users and more than $4.4 trillion in cumulative trading volume.

Pancakeswap (CAKE)
24h7d30d1yAll time

Its services now include perpetual contracts, tokenized stocks, ETFs, yield products, and developer infrastructure. The project is also preparing a dedicated mobile application. Its CAKE ticker and contract address remain unchanged, with existing staking positions unaffected.

Pancake’s relationship with Binance makes this rebrand interesting. Binance Labs announced a strategic investment in CAKE in June 2022. The investment supported the decentralized exchange’s development within the BNB Chain ecosystem.

Coinbase and Binance Compete for the Future of AI Trading

The rivalry becomes clearer when looking beyond the latest announcements. Binance has already introduced its own AI infrastructure through Binance Agent OS. Launched in August 2026, the platform connects compatible AI applications with Binance trading, market data, wallet, and payment capabilities.

Its Model Context Protocol server supports compatible AI agents, including ChatGPT. Developers can build applications that access supported Binance services through user-controlled permissions.

Pancake is also developing its position in this emerging market. In July, the platform partnered with BNB Chain’s Agent Studio to help developers deploy autonomous agents.

These agents can interact with Pancake’s liquidity pools, rebalance positions, and execute trading strategies. Its AI tools also include portfolio planning and assistance across DeFi products.

This creates an interesting contrast between the two ecosystems. Coinbase is bringing AI-powered trading directly to consumers through ChatGPT. Binance is building infrastructure that allows developers and AI agents to interact with its services. Pancake adds a decentralized execution layer to the wider BNB Chain ecosystem.

The next battle in crypto may not be about which exchange attracts the most human traders. It could be about which infrastructure becomes the preferred destination for AI-powered financial activity.

title: Why a 5% Stablecoin Return Can Still Cost Holders Money
description:
Key TakeAways A steady peg doesn’t protect euro value. A 10% euro rise cancels 10% yield. Two conversion fees push […]
The post Why a 5% Stablecoin Return Can Still Cost Holders Money appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key TakeAways

  • A steady peg doesn’t protect euro value.
  • A 10% euro rise cancels 10% yield.
  • Two conversion fees push the hurdle higher.
  • EU rules ban interest on e-money tokens.

In September 2026, the European Banking Authority urged the Commission to consider regulating crypto-asset lending, the kind of business that sits behind stablecoin yields offered to Europeans.

For anyone who swapped euros to earn one, that yield has a catch. Our earlier piece showed why a perfect dollar peg can still cost holders euros. This one works out how much return it takes to cover that gap, where a return can legally come from in the EU, and what the extra dollar yield is really paying for.

A 5% return that ends €455 short

Start with €10,000 and an exchange rate of 1.10, so one euro buys $1.10. Ignore fees for now. The saver receives 11,000 tokens, each redeemable for $1.

A lending product then adds 5% over twelve months, lifting the balance to 11,550 tokens. The peg never slips.

The euro moves instead. By year-end EUR/USD sits at 1.21, and those 11,550 tokens convert back to €9,545.45. That leaves the saver €454.55 down after a year of positive returns.

The currency side of this is the trap our earlier piece walked through: a 10% euro rise cuts a dollar balance’s euro value by about 9.09%. What changes here is the yield. With no return, the saver would have ended at €9,090.91. The 5% claws back half of that damage. Half.

The return you need just to get your euros back

With the peg intact and no costs, one line covers it:

Required return = exit rate ÷ entry rate – 1

Here that’s 1.21 ÷ 1.10 – 1, or 10%. Earn less and the saver loses money in euro terms, however good the dollar figure looks.

Fees lift the bar. Assume 0.5% goes on the way in and another 0.5% on the way out, round numbers chosen for illustration rather than taken from any provider’s price list. Only €9,950 gets converted, buying 10,945 tokens, and the exit fee trims whatever comes back. Both deductions enter the formula:

Required return = (exit rate ÷ entry rate) ÷ (0.995 × 0.995) – 1

At 1.21, the hurdle rises to about 11.11%. The same 5% year now returns €9,450.24. Swap in your own platform’s fees and the formula still works.

Euro weakens to 1.00

No yield, no fees: €11,000.00

5% yield, no fees: €11,550.00

5% yield, with fees: €11,434.79

Yield needed after fees: none

Rate stays at 1.10

No yield, no fees: €10,000.00

5% yield, no fees: €10,500.00

5% yield, with fees: €10,395.26

Yield needed after fees: about 1.01%

Euro strengthens to 1.21

No yield, no fees: €9,090.91

5% yield, no fees: €9,545.45

5% yield, with fees: €9,450.24

Yield needed after fees: about 11.11%

Hypothetical scenarios calculated by the Coindoo team for €10,000 converted at 1.10 and held for one year. Tokens stay at $1, fees are 0.5% per conversion, and the figures exclude taxes and inflation.

A weaker euro gives the saver a currency gain with no yield at all. A flat rate makes fees the main obstacle, small but real. A stronger euro is the case that hurts, and it turns a respectable 5% into a loss.

Real routes rarely cost a neat 0.5%. Trading fees, exchange spreads, network charges and bank fees stack up, and fixed charges bite harder on small balances. Redemption has its own catch. Under Circle’s EEA redemption policy, retail USDC holders need an account that can receive dollars, and Circle warns that banks may charge for incoming payments or currency conversion. A $1 redemption claim tells you very little about the euros that finally land in your account.

Breaking even also has a narrow meaning here: the same number of euros back. It ignores inflation. And it skips the obvious question of what those euros could have earned without ever leaving the currency.

What the extra dollar yield pays for

Dollar returns tend to sit above euro returns because US policy rates do. The Federal Reserve held its target range at 3.75% to 4% on October 28. A day later, the ECB kept its deposit rate at 2.50%.

That gap of roughly 1.25 to 1.5 percentage points isn’t free money. A saver who wanted the dollar return without the currency exposure would have to hedge it, and in currency markets the cost of hedging tracks the interest-rate difference between the two currencies. Economists call this covered interest parity. In plain terms: remove the currency risk and most of the extra yield goes with it.

Skip the hedge and the saver keeps the premium, along with the risk the cards above show. Part of any dollar stablecoin yield above euro rates is payment for carrying that risk, whatever the platform calls it.

Crypto lending rates don’t move one-for-one with central banks. Borrower demand sets them, and they can swing far from policy rates. The currency trade-off stays the same either way.

READ MORE:

The World Bank’s USDC Plan Has a Problem Nobody Mentions

In the EU, the issuer can’t pay you that 5%

So where does a European’s stablecoin return come from? Not from the token. Circle’s EU white paper for USDC describes a token backed by dollar-denominated assets and redeemable 1:1 for dollars. Holding it earns nothing.

MiCA Article 50 closes the obvious shortcut. It bars e-money-token issuers and crypto-asset service providers from granting interest on those tokens, and it counts any reward linked to how long you hold them as interest, whatever the label. A regulated EU exchange can’t pay you for simply keeping USDC in your account.

Any advertised yield therefore points somewhere else: a lending arrangement, a DeFi protocol, or a platform operating outside that rule. Every one of them puts your tokens in someone else’s hands. Ask who borrows them, what secures the loan, whether withdrawals can be paused, and whether the rate is fixed or resets daily. The 5% in our example is a completed year’s return, while an advertised annual rate can change long before the year is out.

That lending business, including activity linked to DeFi, is exactly what the EBA wants brought under rules. MiCA doesn’t cover it today.

When dollars fit, and when EURC makes more sense

None of this makes a dollar balance a mistake. If you have a dollar invoice to pay or dollar income coming in, you already hold the right currency, and the euro rate barely touches you.

Euro spenders face a different test. Circle describes EURC as redeemable 1:1 for euros, which takes the currency mismatch off the table. Switching currency leaves issuer, custody and platform risk where they were. What it removes is the exchange-rate line from the calculation.

Before converting, write down three numbers: the rate you get in at, the total cost of the round trip, and the return the product has actually paid in the past rather than the one on the banner. The yield left after fees is the size of euro rally the balance can absorb. A bigger rally eats the gain, however many tokens you’ve added.

The post Why a 5% Stablecoin Return Can Still Cost Holders Money appeared first on Coindoo.
